tldr: Without using any cameras or external tracking, a robot hand successfully achieved zero-shot transfer of continuous Baoding ball rotation using only joint encoders and 16 binary tactile sensors. The paper reveals that touch does not drive the primary motion, but instead locally resets and corrects disturbances in the periodic movement rhythm to ensure long-term stability.
hero_caption: Overall framework of the proposed method. Tendon coupling structures and tactile sensor layouts are matched to hardware in simulation. Reinforcement learning is performed with slew-rate action limits (SlewDR) and STuck-AT Taxels (STAT), and the resulting policy is directly deployed zero-shot to physical hardware alongside hysteresis calibration.
overview:
In-hand manipulation—dexterously rolling multiple objects inside the hand—is an exceptionally difficult challenge for robots because contacts are continually made and broken. While humans can smoothly rotate Baoding balls (two metal spheres) using only fingertip sensation without vision, conventional robotics research has predominantly relied on tracking object positions using cameras or motion capture. But for in-hand manipulation where objects are occluded by fingers, should we really depend on "external eyes" in the first place?

This study tackles this question head-on. Without any vision or external object-state information, the authors challenged a four-fingered Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite to keep two Baoding balls rotating using only its own joint angles (proprioception) and 16 binary (ON/OFF) contact sensors. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, they introduced accurate replication of the physical tendon coupling mechanism, tactile sensor hysteresis calibration, and two novel domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits (SlewDR) and sensor stuck-at noise (STAT).

When evaluated on hardware, the policy trained purely in simulation transferred zero-shot, completing 112.5 full rotations (225 consecutive $180^{\circ}$ rotations) in a single continuous trial at a fast speed of $\sim 0.36\;	ext{rot/s}$ without dropping the balls. This is the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation, regardless of the sensing modality used. Comparative experiments ablating touch revealed a clean division of labour: proprioception generates the "underlying rhythm," while tactile sensing handles "repairing disrupted ball configurations."
contributions: Built a simulation environment that faithfully replicates the physical mechanical tendon coupling (a nonlinear behaviour where the DIP joint moves only after the PIP joint bends $100^{\circ}$) and sensor placements.
Proposed two novel randomisation techniques: Slew-rate Domain Randomisation (SlewDR) to overcome actuator tracking lag, and STuck-AT Taxels (STAT) to prevent overfitting to specific sensors.

Demonstrated record-breaking zero-shot transfer performance on a physical hand, completing 225 consecutive half-rotations (112.5 full rotations) without drops, completely free of external vision or object state estimation.

Uncovered through tactile presence/absence and ablation experiments that tactile sensing does not drive the motion itself, but acts as a "corrector" to sustain periodic gait patterns and recover from anomalies.

sections.heading: Rotating Two Balls Without Eyes: How Far Can Touch Alone Go?
sections.summary: In-hand manipulation is notoriously hard to control due to continuous contact changes, and prior work typically relied on cameras to measure object positions directly. This paper investigates whether a robot can achieve zero-shot continuous rotation of interacting Baoding balls using only internal sensations (joint encoders and 16 binary contact signals), just like a human.
sections.details:
In in-hand manipulation, fingertips repeatedly make and break contact, making the system discontinuous and extremely difficult to model. Moreover, because the hand acts as both actuator and sensor, simply moving a finger to correct a position fundamentally alters subsequent contact states. As a result, many prior works have relied on external cameras, markers, or privileged object-pose information inside simulators.

However, when humans manipulate keys or coins in the palm, they do not stare at them. Contact sensations alone provide sufficient understanding of object states. The authors therefore posed a fundamental question: "Can contact information alone substitute for explicit object pose?"

The chosen benchmark task is rotating Baoding balls, a traditional Chinese health tool. Unlike rotating a single object, two balls collide and circulate over the hand, requiring the relative position (phase) of the objects to be maintained without seeing them directly. While there have been successes in simulation, zero-shot transfer to hardware without physical fine-tuning has remained an open challenge. By accurately incorporating the physical tendon-drive characteristics into simulation and introducing unique domain randomisations, the authors set out to crack this problem on physical hardware.

sections.heading: Beyond Vision: The Evolution of Blind Manipulation and Baoding Tasks
sections.summary: While reinforcement learning and domain randomisation have advanced dexterous manipulation, most methods still rely on external cameras. Meanwhile, "blind manipulation" using only joint sensors or touch has succeeded on single objects, but hardware success on multi-object Baoding ball rotation has been extremely limited.
sections.details:
Dexterous robot hand manipulation has progressed rapidly through combinations of simulation-based reinforcement learning (RL) and domain randomisation (training while perturbing environment parameters), exemplified by OpenAI's Rubik's cube work. However, many of these approaches depend on point clouds or object pose information from external cameras, carrying an inherent vulnerability to occlusion when fingers hide the objects.

This sparked interest in "blind manipulation" without external sensors. While studies emerged rotating dice using proprioception alone (joint angles and torques), multi-object manipulation of light, smooth objects like Baoding balls produces joint torque changes that are too subtle to detect, making direct tactile contact sensing indispensable. On the other hand, camera-based high-density optical tactile sensors are difficult to simulate and calibrate, presenting major barriers to real-world transfer.

Looking at hardware Baoding ball manipulation, only a few works existed, combining stereo cameras with model predictive control or depth cameras with FSRs (force-sensing resistors). In terms of touch-only hardware Baoding rotation, one prior work used a 653-element tactile array, but achieved only a single qualitative $180^{\circ}$ rotation. Sustained, high-speed physical demonstrations running for minutes without drops were non-existent.

captions.F2: The physical Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite (left) and the simulation model (right) used in experiments. Twelve FSRs (red) are placed on high-contact areas of the palm and joints, and four BioTac sensors (cyan) are mounted on the fingertips, providing a total of 16 channels of binary contact feedback.

sections.heading: Aligning Sim to Real: Faithful Kinematics and Two Novel Randomisations
sections.summary: The problem is formulated as a POMDP, faithfully incorporating the tendon-coupled sequential finger joint movement into simulation. In addition, "SlewDR" to model motor lag, "STAT" to prevent sensor over-reliance, and hysteresis-based tactile calibration were introduced.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-B Problem Formulation and Agent Architecture
The task is to continuously rotate two smooth Baoding balls (diameter $\sim 4\;	ext{cm}$ / $1.58\;	ext{inches}$, mass $55\;	ext{g}$) in the hand without dropping them. The agent receives observations from the past 4 frames. Each frame contains the joint positions, velocities, tracking errors, and previous actions of 13 actuators (52 dimensions total), alongside 16 channels of binary tactile signals—a very compact 272-dimensional input. There are no cameras or privileged information. The policy outputs 13-dimensional target joint positions at 60 Hz and is trained via PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) in Isaac Lab.

### III-C & III-D Physical Platform and Simulation Kinematics Alignment
The robot hand used is the four-fingered Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite. The proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the index, middle, and ring fingers are mechanically coupled via tendons. Here, the authors made a critical finding: while the default Isaac Lab model used a linear coupling where the DIP bends simultaneously with the PIP at a fixed ratio, the actual hardware exhibits a sequential nonlinear behaviour where the DIP joint only starts bending after the PIP reaches approximately $100^{\circ}$. They corrected this kinematic gap by implementing control logic in simulation that replicates the exact physical flexion and extension sequence.

### III-E Novel Techniques Bridging the Sim-to-Real Gap
Even with kinematics aligned, gaps in friction and actuator delays remain. These were bridged via the following methods:
- **Physical Parameter Randomisation**: Ball mass ($45\sim 100\;	ext{g}$) and friction coefficients were randomised per episode. Friction was set high for the fingertip BioTac silicone skin and low for the palm.
- **SlewDR (Slew-rate Domain Randomisation)**: On hardware, tendon friction and motor inertia prevent tracking rapid command changes. The authors imposed a per-step action delta limit (slew-rate limit) and randomly sampled its scale $s$ from a uniform distribution $0.3 \sim 1.0$ per episode during training. This limit was also applied as a fixed value during hardware deployment, preventing aggressive oscillations.
- **STAT (STuck-AT Taxels)**: Training on clean tactile data causes policies to become overly reliant on specific channels. The authors introduced stuck-at noise (STAT), randomly choosing $k$ taxels out of the 12 FSRs and fixing their values to either ON or OFF for entire episodes. This trains the policy to remain robust even when sensors malfunction.
- **Hysteresis Tactile Calibration**: Physical FSR baselines drift due to wire movement and hand posture. Using the median $	ext{med}(x)$ and 99.5th percentile $P_{99.5}(x)$ of idle hand readings, two separate high/low thresholds (a Schmitt-trigger principle) were established to binarise signals without chattering.

captions.F3: Comparison of tendon-driven joint coupling mechanisms. Left shows the corrected behaviour in this work, where the DIP joint moves only after the PIP joint fully bends, matching hardware. Right shows Isaac Lab's default behaviour, where both joints bend simultaneously, causing a major discrepancy with the physical hand.

sections.heading: Uncompromising Testing: Zero-Shot Deployment Protocol and Evaluation Metrics
sections.summary: Policies trained in simulation were deployed directly to hardware without fine-tuning or checkpoint cherry-picking. Each trial continued indefinitely until a drop, rigorously measuring continuous rotations, time to drop, rotation speed, and gait efficiency.
sections.details:
### IV-A Evaluation Protocol
The physical Shadow Hand Lite was mounted tilted downward at approximately $15^{\circ}$ from horizontal and controlled at 60 Hz. Real-world PD gains were kept fixed (with select gains lowered post-testing) across all conditions. Crucially, this was a strict zero-shot deployment: no fine-tuning, adaptation, or cherry-picking of checkpoints based on physical performance was performed. Ten independent trials were conducted per condition, running without time limits until the balls dropped from the hand.

Evaluated baselines included "C3" (the full proposed randomisation pipeline), "C2" (without STAT), "C1" (baseline without SlewDR or STAT), "Proprio-only" (trained without touch), "C3-TacOff" (trained C3 with tactile inputs zeroed on hardware), and "Open-loop" (replaying fixed trajectories).

### IV-B Evaluation Metrics
Performance was measured using four hardware metrics:
- **Full Rotations**: Exchanging the positions of the two balls twice equals one full $360^{\circ}$ rotation. The number of full rotations completed before dropping was counted.
- **Time to Drop ($t_{	ext{drop}}$)**: Duration in seconds from placing the balls on the hand until they drop.
- **Rotational Speed**: Rotations per second (rot/s) during the first 10 seconds.
- **Swap Efficiency ($\eta$)**: The fraction of finger gait cycles that resulted in successful ball swaps. Defined as $\eta =  rac{R_{10}}{f_{	ext{gait}} T}$, reaching an optimal 1.0 if balls swap on every single cycle without missing.

sections.heading: 112 Consecutive Rotations: The Staggering Hardware Performance of Touch and Randomisation
sections.summary: The proposed method (C3) dominated with a 10-trial average of 34.75 rotations and a 94.8-second survival time. In a single endurance demonstration, it completed 112.5 full rotations (225 half-rotations) across 310 continuous seconds without a single drop, setting a world record.
sections.details:
Across the 10-trial hardware benchmark, the proposed method (C3) won by a wide margin. C3 achieved an average of 34.75 full rotations, a drop time of 94.8 s, and a rotation speed of 0.360 rot/s. All 10 trials survived past 2 rotations, and 9 survived past 10 seconds. In contrast, C1 (standard randomisation) managed only 0.35 rotations, and C2 (adding only SlewDR) reached just 0.50 rotations, both dropping the balls within 5 to 6 seconds. While C1 and C2 spun rapidly in simulation, they failed completely upon hardware transfer.

The critical role of touch was also laid bare. When tactile inputs to the C3 policy were forced to zero on hardware (C3-TacOff), average rotations plummeted from 34.75 to just 5.00, and drop time crashed to 19.0 s. The Proprio-only baseline trained without touch averaged only 4.40 rotations, while open-loop replay lasted only 1.70 rotations.

Furthermore, in an extended endurance demonstration conducted separately from the 10-trial benchmark, C3 operated continuously for 310 seconds without dropping the balls once, completing 112.5 full rotations (225 consecutive $180^{\circ}$ swaps). This stands as the highest hardware result reported for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed, outperforming all prior works regardless of whether vision or touch was used.

captions.F5: Comparison of joint trajectories across four gait cycles. Top: In proprioception-only (blue: balls present, red: no balls), joint trajectories match almost identically regardless of object presence, indicating blind execution of a fixed motion. Bottom: In C3 (blue: touch enabled, red: touch zeroed), trajectory peaks vary across cycles when touch is active, confirming adaptive motion adjustments in response to contact.

sections.heading: What Does Touch Really Contribute? "Muscles" Keep Rhythm, "Skin" Prevents Collapse
sections.summary: Even without touch, fingers keep moving at the same frequency, but drop the balls easily. The essence of touch is not motion generation; rather, it corrects offsets in the proprioceptive base gait and ensures swap execution. Combining SlewDR and STAT was the key to transfer success.
sections.details:
### VI-A What Does Touch Provide?
In both C3-TacOff and Proprio-only, the fingers continued oscillating at a rapid rhythm of approximately 8 cycles. Even when balls were removed so fingers swung in empty air, joint trajectories barely changed. This indicates that the policy uses proprioception alone to replay a learned, fixed periodic pattern (gait).

So what does touch do? When touch is enabled in C3, swap efficiency $\eta$ surges to 0.90 (close to the theoretical limit of 1.0). With touch, joint amplitudes dynamically adapt across cycles; when a ball drifts out of position, recovery motions emerge—such as cradling the ball with the thumb while other fingers realign it. In short, proprioception provides the primary driving rhythm, while touch serves as a "local corrector" pulling the balls back into the cycle whenever they drift.

### VI-B How Randomisation Enabled Transfer
C1 achieved blistering speeds of 1 rotation per second in simulation, but physical joints could not track the commands, leading to immediate failure. Introducing SlewDR in C2 cut out high-frequency action chatter, enabling the policy to learn smooth trajectories aligned with physical limits.

However, while C2 produced smooth motions, it became hyper-dependent on tactile cues, showing a nearly 60% drop rate in simulation when touch was muted. Adding STAT forced taxel values to freeze during training, compelling the policy to adopt a healthy division of labour: delegate base locomotion to proprioception and use touch as an auxiliary guide. This yielded robustness against contact sensing errors and enabled reliable real-world transfer.

### VI-C How Much Tactile Information Is Needed?
A spatial mismatch existed between simulation and hardware regarding which sensors fired most frequently. Despite this discrepancy, transfer succeeded. This demonstrates that high-resolution tactile images and pin-point sensor alignment are unnecessary; coarse, binary contact signals across broad regions are entirely sufficient to stabilise in-hand manipulation.

captions.F7: Comparison of policy action targets (top) and measured joint positions (bottom) on hardware. In C1 (left), targets oscillate violently at high frequencies, preventing the hand from tracking them. In C2 with SlewDR (right), targets are smooth and the physical hand tracks them faithfully.
captions.F8: Normalised firing frequency of binary tactile sensors in simulation (left) and hardware (right). In simulation, sensors on the middle segments of the middle/ring fingers fire most, whereas proximal sensors respond more on hardware. Despite this spatial mismatch, sparse binary contact signals transfer successfully.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Outlook: A New Era for Blind Tactile Manipulation
sections.summary: The authors proved that zero-shot hardware transfer of continuous Baoding ball manipulation is achievable using only joint feedback and binary contact sensors without vision. Touch fine-tunes the rhythmic gait driven by proprioception, opening paths to manipulating varied sizes and irregular shapes in the future.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated that the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite can stably rotate Baoding balls using only in-hand proprioception and 16 channels of binary contact sensing, without cameras or external object tracking. A simulation design accurately capturing hardware kinematics, hysteresis tactile calibration, and two novel domain randomisations (SlewDR and STAT) underpinned the record-breaking hardware performance of 112.5 continuous full rotations (225 consecutive swaps).

Crucially, the research identified a clear separation of roles: proprioception sustains the periodic motion pattern, while binary touch guides that pattern to success and recovers from anomalies. This highlights the true value of tactile sensing in in-hand manipulation where vision is prone to occlusion.

For future work, the authors outline generalizing across different ball sizes and masses, manipulating irregular non-spherical shapes, and investigating blind zero-shot transfer using denser tactile sensor arrays.

takeaways: Do not blindly trust default simulator robot models; correcting nonlinear kinematic properties like tendon-coupling sequences to match hardware is the essential first step for Sim-to-Real success.
Actuator tracking lag and violent command chattering can be drastically alleviated by SlewDR, which randomly limits action slew rates during training.

Over-reliance on tactile feedback impairs real-world transfer; deliberately freezing sensor values with STAT enforces a robust division of labour where proprioception drives the gait and touch handles corrections.

Sophisticated in-hand manipulation does not strictly require high-precision camera tracking; sparse binary contact signals paired with joint encoders can sustain manipulation with remarkable robustness.
limitations: Evaluation was restricted to two identical smooth spheres (1.58-inch diameter, 55 g mass); generalization to varied sizes or heterogeneous shapes remains untested.
Experiments were conducted in a fixed pose with the palm tilted $15^{\circ}$ downward, meaning robustness under dynamic hand movement and shifting gravity vectors is not guaranteed.
Attempts at dynamic calibration to compensate for wire-motion baseline drift in the FSRs did not yield consistent improvements and were excluded from the final pipeline.
